Authorisation asks what that identity may do, and that is expressed in SQL as privileges granted to roles. In PostgreSQL, a user is simply a role that is allowed to log in. The first card shows two roles that differ only in that attribute. The second card shows a session acting as the analyst role. The third card shows the default: a brand-new role has no rights at all, so even a qualified query on the orders table is refused with permission denied for the schema. With an unqualified name you would get a does not exist message instead, because objects in a schema you may not use are invisible. The owner of an object, whoever created it, may do everything with it. So logging in grants nothing by itself: identity comes first, and privileges are explicit. The roles here are created inside a transaction that is rolled back, so nothing is left in the database.

Privileges are granted per object and per action. The first card creates the analyst role, grants usage on the schema, select on orders and customers, and insert on orders, then acts as the analyst: counting orders returns eleven. The second card is a permission matrix, built with the has table privilege function. For orders, the analyst may select and insert but not update or delete; for customers only select; for payments nothing at all. The matrix is the picture a reviewer needs, because individual grants are hard to add up. The third card shows an action that was never granted: updating an order is refused with permission denied for the table. The fourth card shows revoke: after the select privilege is taken back, even reading is refused. Reading does not imply writing, and every action is a separate privilege. The runner is a superuser, so acting as the role with set role is what makes these checks real. Everything is rolled back afterwards.

Granting privileges person by person does not scale, so we grant them to group roles and make people members. The graph shows two group roles: readers can select from every table, and writers can insert and update orders. Ana is a member of readers; the clerk is a member of both. Membership inherits the privileges, and the matrix for orders confirms it: ana can only select, while the clerk can select, insert and update, but not delete. The third card shows the least-privilege principle in action: the clerk's update succeeds, and the delete is refused because nobody was given delete, since no job needs it. The table lists the design rules: grant to roles rather than people, one role per job, only what the job needs, and review the matrix, because privileges tend to accumulate. More privileges feel safer for an application, but they widen every mistake. That is a design judgement, and it depends on the real jobs in your organisation, not on this small shop alone.

There are two common ways to limit what a role can see. A view restricts columns. The first card creates a view of customer contacts without email or phone, grants it to the analyst, and the analyst can read the view but is refused on the customers table itself. By default a view runs with the rights of its owner, which is why this works; a security invoker option, from PostgreSQL fifteen, makes it use the caller's rights instead. A row-level policy restricts rows, and it is declared on the table. In the second card, a policy says a sales role sees only the orders whose employee matches a session setting. Employee four sees orders one, five and ten; employee five sees three and seven; and the owner still sees all eleven, because owners and superusers bypass policies. The warning tile is a lesson: the six online orders have no employee, so they match nobody. A policy that returns rows is not proof it is correct; check who it hides, and always test as the restricted role.

Query text built by pasting user input is a security boundary problem. The first card pastes the input x quote or quote one equals quote one into the where clause, and the input becomes code: all nine customers come back. The second card passes the very same text as a parameter of a prepared statement. A normal address finds customer one, and the hostile text is just a value that matches nobody. Prepare and execute is the server-side equivalent of the placeholders that database drivers send. A parameter can only stand for a value. The third card shows that a table name cannot be a parameter, which is a syntax error, so names from outside must be checked against an allowlist or quoted with the format function and its identifier option, as the fourth card shows. Finally, the application should connect with a role that has only the privileges it needs, as a second layer: it may insert an order, but delete is refused. Separate values from code first; narrow privileges limit the damage if something is missed.

This closing case follows one shop from design to controlled access. The chips mark where each chapter shows up. The tables, keys and constraints of chapters one and two make an order possible and refuse impossible ones. The first card places order twelve for Ben: insert the order and its line from chapter three, decrement the stock with a guarded update, as chapter nine taught, and read the order back through a join from chapter five, giving a total of fifty-nine eighty. The second card answers a business question with a common table expression and a window function: Dev leads with twelve hundred five, then Ben, then Asha. Chapter seven would ask what that query costs. The third card applies chapter ten: a support role sees order counts by status through a view, while the email column stays closed. Each choice had a reason, and the reasons are what we have tried to explain. This course illustrates reasoning on one small database, and it does not verify that anyone has gained practical competence. Continue exploring unfamiliar queries, documented engine differences, and failure cases; practical competence requires separate implementation experience.
